## Quantitative Calibration {#sec-calibration}

This section maps the model parameters to the AI infrastructure sector using publicly available data from company filings, industry reports, and the scaling laws literature.
The calibration is *stylized*: the goal is to discipline the model's quantitative magnitudes and illustrate cross-sectional heterogeneity, not to structurally estimate firm-level primitives or test the model empirically.
Two caveats should be noted at the outset.
First, the Leland default framework is an analytically tractable approximation to financial distress risk; it fits public-debt issuers better than VC-backed labs, though the qualitative predictions apply across financing structures (see @sec-discussion). As AI labs mature, the Leland setting is becoming more literal: OpenAI secured a \$4B revolving credit facility in October 2024,^[\url{https://www.cnbc.com/2024/10/03/openai-gets-4-billion-revolving-credit-line-on-top-of-latest-funding.html}.] xAI arranged \$5B+ in secured notes and term loans, and hyperscalers issued \$121B in bonds in 2025 alone.
Second, the training fractions $\hat{\phi}$ are inferred from incomplete data and carry substantial uncertainty ($\pm 0.10$).
The calibration proceeds in three steps: I first set the demand process parameters, then the technology and cost parameters, and finally the financial parameters.

@tbl-parameters in the Internet Appendix summarizes the calibration status of each parameter.

### Demand Process

The demand process parameters govern the drift and volatility of AI compute demand under each regime.
I use regime-dependent drifts $\mu_L = 0.01$ and $\mu_H = 0.06$, with common volatility $\sigma = 0.25$.
The low-regime drift captures baseline growth in cloud computing revenue; the high-regime drift reflects the substantially higher growth that would characterize a world in which transformative AI capabilities generate massive new demand.
Both drifts are *risk-adjusted* (certainty-equivalent) growth rates, not observed revenue growth: the cloud revenue growth of 24--39\% cited in @tbl-sources is consistent with a much lower $\mu_H$ once the substantial risk premium embedded in $r$ is netted out, and the convergence requirement $r > \mu_H$ bounds the admissible value from above.
Because the implied risk adjustment cannot be measured directly, $\mu_H = 0.06$ is best read as a disciplined choice (its status in @tbl-parameters is "Chosen") rather than an empirical estimate.
The common volatility $\sigma = 0.25$ is a chosen proxy rather than a measured moment: the demand shifter $X$ is a latent risk-adjusted state variable, and its closest observable analogue---quarterly revenue growth of cloud providers---is smoothed by multi-year contracts and revenue-recognition rules, so it disciplines the order of magnitude without identifying $\sigma$ (its status in @tbl-parameters is "Chosen").
The interior-capacity condition (A2) discussed below admits $\sigma \in (0.19, 0.39)$ at the baseline values of the remaining parameters, and $\sigma = 0.25$ sits comfortably inside that window.

The arrival rate $\lambda = 0.10$ per year implies an expected time to regime switch of 10 years.
This baseline represents a moderate prior, intended to approximate the marginal investor's belief rather than any particular executive's view.
It is more conservative than the beliefs implied by @amodei2024machines ($\lambda \approx 0.30$--$0.50$) or Hassabis ($\lambda \approx 0.10$--$0.15$), and the dispersion across these views is precisely what generates the cross-sectional variation in investment behavior analyzed in @sec-valuation.

The baseline discount rate is $r = 0.12$, the risk-adjusted WACC for a representative frontier AI lab.
As discussed in @sec-model ([Footnote \ref{fn:wacc}]{.content-visible when-format="pdf"}[the footnote on risk-adjusted discounting]{.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}), $r$ is the WACC and $\mu_s$ is the risk-adjusted growth rate (the physical drift minus an appropriate risk premium, so that discounting expected cash flows at $r$ yields the correct present value); all valuation uses this reduced-form framework throughout.
The baseline exceeds typical corporate WACCs because frontier AI labs carry substantial technology risk and are typically high-growth with elevated cost of equity; industry estimates give WACCs of 7.2\% for computer software and 10.8\% for semiconductors,^[\url{https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/wacc.htm}.] and CAPM-based estimates for private AI labs with market betas of 1.5--2.5 yield a cost of equity of approximately 10.5--15.0\%.
The analytical results and figures in @sec-model use $r = 0.12$ throughout; these illustrate model properties at a representative WACC and do not correspond to any specific firm archetype.
The firm-specific WACCs in @tbl-firms (ranging from 0.10 to 0.18) play a narrower role than a full cross-sectional sensitivity analysis would, for a reason that belongs in the main text rather than the Internet Appendix.
The interior-capacity condition (A2), $1/\gamma < (\beta_H - 1)/(\alpha\beta_H) < 1$, depends on $r$ through the characteristic root $\beta_H$, and at the baseline values of the remaining parameters it admits only $r \in (0.097, 0.135)$.
The Google-like hyperscaler ($r = 0.10$) and the baseline ($r = 0.12$) lie inside this window; the platform ($r = 0.14$), the frontier lab ($r = 0.15$), and the compute racer ($r = 0.18$) violate its upper bound.
When that bound fails the capacity problem has no interior optimum---the option-value factor diverges as $K \to 0$---so the solvers verify (A2) before optimizing and raise an error rather than report a boundary artifact (Internet Appendix B).
Archetype-specific WACCs accordingly enter the analysis through one channel only: the capacity-free training-allocation inversion $\lambda = (\hat{\phi}/(1-\hat{\phi}))^{1-\alpha}(r - \mu_H)$ reported later in this section.
Every trigger and capacity result in the paper is computed at the baseline WACC, and the sensitivity sweeps vary $r$ inside the admissible window.

### Technology Parameters

The revenue elasticity $\alpha = 0.40$ governs diminishing returns to capacity in revenue generation, entering both the L-regime inference contest (@eq-contest-L) and the H-regime training contest (@eq-contest-H); the compute-to-loss power laws in @kaplan2020scaling and @hoffmann2022training motivate the choice of a concave revenue technology, but they do not measure $\alpha$---a loss exponent is not a revenue elasticity, and no public series maps compute to revenue at the firm level, so $\alpha = 0.40$ is a chosen value (@tbl-parameters).
Holding contest share fixed (or in the single-firm case), doubling the relevant capacity measure increases revenue by approximately $2^{0.4} \approx 1.32$ times---a 32\% increase rather than 100\%---reflecting diminishing returns to scale.
In a symmetric duopoly, a unilateral doubling also raises the contest share, so the total revenue gain is larger (approximately 50\% at baseline).
Two limitations of this choice should be disclosed.
First, condition (A2) admits only $\alpha \in (0.356, 0.534)$ at the baseline values of the remaining parameters, so $\alpha = 0.40$ sits close to the lower bound; numerical optimization does not relax the restriction, because the joint optimization over $(\log K, \phi)$ verifies (A2) first and raises an error when it fails, so all sensitivity ranges are truncated to the admissible window (Internet Appendix B).
Second, the trigger and capacity are highly sensitive to $\alpha$ within that window---elasticities of $+19.7$ and $+24.2$ (@tbl-elasticities)---which is why the paper reports ratios and percentage differences rather than levels, and why the archetype table below is read as an illustrative cross-section rather than as a set of estimated firm-level primitives.
The cost function $I(K) = cK^\gamma$ with convexity $\gamma = 1.50$ captures increasing marginal costs from power constraints, supply chain bottlenecks (particularly for advanced GPUs), and site preparation costs; I normalize the unit cost $c = 1.0$, so all monetary values are interpreted relative to this normalization.

The operating cost rate $\delta = 0.03$ represents the ongoing cost of maintaining installed capacity---power, cooling, maintenance, and personnel---expressed as a fraction of capacity per year, distinct from both accounting depreciation and economic depreciation of GPU hardware.
Accounting depreciation for data center equipment typically implies a 3--5 year useful life (20--33\% per year), and power costs alone can reach \$0.05--0.10/kWh at hyperscale.
In the model, the *capital* cost of hardware is captured in $cK^\gamma$; $\delta$ captures only the *operating* flow cost.
Economic depreciation through technological obsolescence (e.g., H100$\to$B200 transitions) would justify a higher effective $\delta$.
Nothing substantive turns on the choice, for a reason worth making precise.
Because $\delta$ enters only through the total cost $b(K) = \delta K/r + cK^\gamma$ and revenue is a pure power of capacity, a change in $\delta$ is exactly equivalent to a rescaling of the capacity unit: replacing $(\delta, K)$ by $(\delta s^{1-\gamma}, K/s)$ leaves the optimization problem unchanged up to a constant factor.
The elasticities of $+2.2$ for the trigger and $+2.0$ for capacity in @tbl-elasticities are exactly the exponents of that rescaling, $(\gamma - \alpha)/(\gamma - 1)$ and $1/(\gamma - 1)$, rather than economic sensitivity.
Recomputing the model at $\delta = 0.10$ confirms this: the levels move ($X^*$ from $0.0047$ to $0.0667$, $K^*$ from $0.0067$ to $0.0747$), while $\phi^* = 0.70$, the preemption discount $X_P / X_L^{\text{mono}} = 0.57$, the follower-to-leader capacity ratio, and the Dario's dilemma losses (26.2\% conservative versus 5.6\% aggressive) are numerically identical to their baseline values.
The calibrated $\delta$ is therefore part of the cost normalization rather than a separately identified quantity, which is also why the industry operating-cost estimates in @tbl-sources---an annual burden of 30--40\% of hardware capital expenditure---do not contradict $\delta = 0.03$: the model's $\delta$ is a flow per unit of the abstract capacity index $K$, whose scale is fixed by the normalization $c = 1$, not per dollar of installed hardware.
The one class of reported quantities that is not invariant in this sense is the credit spreads and default probabilities of @sec-valuation, which are evaluated at a fixed $(X, K)$ rather than at the optimal policy.

### Stylized Firm Archetypes

I construct four stylized firm archetypes representing the major categories of frontier AI labs.
These archetypes are designed to span the relevant cross-sectional variation in investment intensity, leverage, and training allocation; they are *illustrative composites*, not structural estimates of any specific company's parameters.

| Parameter | Frontier Lab | Platform | Hyperscaler | Compute Racer |
|:----------|:------------|:---------|:------------|:--------------|
| Archetype | Anthropic | OpenAI | Google | xAI |
| Revenue 2024 (\$B) | 0.9 | 3.7 | 43.0 | 0.2 |
| Revenue 2025 (\$B) | 4.5 | 12.5 | 60.0 | 0.5 |
| CapEx 2025 (\$B) | 3.0 | 12.0 | 91.0 | 10.0 |
| CapEx / Revenue | 0.67 | 0.96 | 1.52 | 20.0 |
| Leverage | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.10 | 0.15 |
| WACC | 0.15 | 0.14 | 0.10 | 0.18 |
| Training fraction $\hat{\phi}$ | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.35 | 0.75 |

: Stylized firm parameters. Revenue from AI-related activities; CapEx includes cloud compute commitments (Anthropic, OpenAI) and total infrastructure spending (Google, xAI). Training fractions estimated from executive statements [@amodei2026dwarkesh], the Epoch AI compute analysis, and Deloitte's TMT Predictions 2026. All figures are order-of-magnitude composites, not precise calibrations. {#tbl-firms tbl-colwidths="[24,15,15,15,15]"}

The figures in @tbl-firms are approximate composites derived from public filings (10-K, 10-Q), earnings call guidance, press reports, and analyst estimates (see @tbl-sources for details).
For the Anthropic-like archetype, 2025 revenue of \$4.5B reflects collected revenue, not the annualized run rate (\$9B ARR at year-end 2025, accelerating to \$14B ARR by February 2026); CapEx reflects annual cloud compute commitments, primarily on AWS (\$2.66B through September 2025) and Google Cloud TPUs.
For the OpenAI-like archetype, 2024 revenue of \$3.7B and 2025 revenue of \$12.5B follow the CFO's January 2026 disclosure (\$20B ARR at year-end); CapEx of \$12B reflects Azure inference and training spend, which Epoch AI decomposes as approximately \$3B training, \$2B research/experimentation, and \$1.8B inference for 2024 alone.^[\url{https://epoch.ai/data-insights/openai-compute-spend}.]
For the Google-like archetype, revenue is Google Cloud revenue (\$43.2B in 2024, growing 37--39\% to \$59--60B in 2025 per the Alphabet SEC filing), not Alphabet-wide revenue (\$403B); CapEx is total Alphabet capital expenditure (\$91.4B in 2025), approximately 60\% to servers and 40\% to data centers and networking.
The resulting CapEx/Revenue ratio of 1.52$\times$ intentionally uses consolidated CapEx as the numerator because the majority of Alphabet's infrastructure spending supports AI workloads across all products, not only the Cloud segment; a segment-level ratio using only Cloud-attributed CapEx would be lower (approximately 0.5--0.7$\times$) but would understate the total AI infrastructure investment that the model's capacity $K$ represents.
For the xAI-like archetype,^[This illustration relies on xAI figures from before the firm's acquisition by SpaceX, announced in February 2026 at a combined valuation of \$1.25 trillion (\url{https://www.reuters.com/business/musks-spacex-merge-with-xai-combined-valuation-125-trillion-bloomberg-news-2026-02-02/}); the archetype is calibrated to xAI as a standalone frontier lab as of Q4 2025--Q1 2026.] revenue reflects standalone AI-related revenue (Grok API and subscriptions); Bloomberg reported Q3 2025 revenue of \$107M, roughly doubled quarter-on-quarter. The March 2025 merger with X complicates attribution, but standalone AI figures best match the model's scope.
The same sector-specific revenue concept applies to all archetypes: revenue from AI-related activities, not diversified corporate totals.
For privately held firms (the Anthropic-like and xAI-like archetypes), figures are based on press reports and carry lower confidence than publicly disclosed data; they should be treated as order-of-magnitude estimates.
Because the revenue and CapEx concepts are not harmonized across the four archetypes---sector revenue versus segment revenue, cloud commitments versus owned infrastructure---the columns of @tbl-firms should be read one at a time as inputs to the model, not compared with each other as measured cross-sectional moments; the discussion below therefore describes the dispersion qualitatively.
The qualitative results are robust to moderate perturbation of these inputs within the admissible parameter region (@tbl-elasticities; Internet Appendix E).

The training fraction $\hat{\phi}$ estimates reflect the approximate share of compute allocated to model training versus inference serving.
These estimates are inherently uncertain, as firms do not publicly disclose precise training-inference breakdowns; the values in @tbl-firms are triangulated from three types of evidence.

*Executive statements.* @amodei2026dwarkesh modeled the long-run equilibrium at "roughly 50/50 training and inference," noting that "it's not gonna be 10\%, it's not gonna be 90\%." Microsoft's CFO described Azure AI revenue as "primarily inference and post-training workloads." Jensen Huang estimated that inference workloads would require "easily 100 times more" compute than anticipated, with inference already exceeding 40\% of AI revenue by late 2025.

*Firm-specific data.* The only company-level decomposition with primary documentation is Epoch AI's analysis of OpenAI's 2024 compute: of approximately \$7B in total cloud compute, roughly \$3B went to training, \$2B to research and experimentation, and \$1.8B to inference. Combined R\&D (training plus research) was approximately 71\%, inference approximately 26\%. The key finding is that "the majority of OpenAI's R\&D compute was likely allocated to research and experimental training runs, rather than the final training runs of released models"---the model's $\hat{\phi}$ subsumes both.

*Industry trajectory.* Deloitte's TMT Predictions 2026 estimates that the industry-wide split shifted from roughly two-thirds training to parity (approximately 50/50) in 2025, and is projected to reach two-thirds inference by 2026, driven by expanding user bases, reasoning models using 10--100 times more compute per query, and enterprise adoption at scale.^[\url{https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/technology-media-and-telecom-predictions.html}.]

The xAI-like compute racer allocates the most to training ($\hat{\phi} = 0.75$), consistent with its strategy of dedicating owned compute (the Colossus supercluster) to frontier model training while outsourcing inference to cloud providers.^[\url{https://x.com/elonmusk/status/1947701807389515912}.]
The Google-like hyperscaler allocates the least ($\hat{\phi} = 0.35$), reflecting its need to serve inference to billions of users across Search, Gmail, and YouTube; Google's seventh-generation Ironwood TPU is explicitly designed for inference workloads.
The Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like archetypes fall between these extremes.
These estimates carry substantial uncertainty---plausibly $\pm 0.10$ for each archetype---and readers should treat them as order-of-magnitude discipline rather than precise moments for structural identification.
The moderate elasticity of $\phi^*$ with respect to $\lambda$ ($\varepsilon \approx +0.5$ at baseline, reflecting $\varepsilon_{\phi^*,\lambda} = (1-\phi^*)/(1-\alpha)$) means that $\phi^*$ varies slowly with $\lambda$, so the inverse mapping $\lambda(\hat{\phi})$ is steep: modest uncertainty in the observed training fraction ($\pm 0.10$) translates into a wide range of implied arrival rates. Inverting the closed-form allocation FOC, $\lambda = (\hat{\phi}/(1-\hat{\phi}))^{1-\alpha}(r - \mu_H)$, for each archetype at $\hat{\phi} \pm 0.10$ yields implied arrival rates that span roughly a factor of two (e.g., the xAI-like archetype implies $\lambda \in [0.09, 0.17]$, corresponding to expected horizons of 6--11 years, while the Google-like hyperscaler implies $\lambda \in [0.03, 0.05]$, or 19--32 years).
Two qualifications apply.
First, the inversion holds the discount rate at the common baseline $r = 0.12$; because the implied $\lambda$ scales with $r - \mu_H$, using archetype-specific WACCs would shift the levels materially (the xAI-like archetype at $r = 0.18$ implies $\lambda \in [0.17, 0.34]$, while the Google-like archetype at $r = 0.10$ implies $\lambda \in [0.02, 0.04]$)---in this case widening, rather than narrowing, the cross-sectional dispersion.
Second, the ordering claim should be read as applying to common perturbations of the $\hat{\phi}$ estimates: the point-estimate ordering xAI-like $>$ OpenAI-like $>$ Anthropic-like $>$ Google-like in implied $\lambda$ is preserved when all $\hat{\phi}$ shift together, but the $\pm 0.10$ bands of adjacent archetypes overlap, so independent errors could reorder neighboring pairs (though not the endpoints).
The cross-sectional variation ($\hat{\phi}$ ranging from 0.35 to 0.75) is more informative than any individual point estimate, and the qualitative results are robust to moderate perturbation of these values (@tbl-elasticities).

An important caveat: the boundary between "training" and "inference" is blurring.
Inference-time scaling---chain-of-thought reasoning, search-augmented generation, and agentic workflows---uses inference hardware to produce capability improvements that were previously achievable only through training.^[\url{https://x.com/polynoamial/status/1834280425457426689}.]
The model treats $\hat{\phi}$ as a fixed allocation at investment time; in practice, firms dynamically reallocate GPUs between training and inference on timescales of weeks (see @sec-discussion for the direction of bias from this simplification).

@fig-firm-comparison provides a visual summary of the calibration targets: panel (a) plots capital expenditure over revenue, and panel (b) places each archetype in revenue-multiple versus leverage space.
Note that the CapEx concept differs across archetypes: for the private labs, it captures cloud compute commitments rather than owned infrastructure, so the ratios in panel (a) are not directly comparable.
Panel (b) reveals substantial dispersion---the Anthropic-like lab combines a $5.0\times$ revenue multiple with minimal leverage, while the Google-like hyperscaler combines the most modest multiple with the lowest cost of capital---and this dispersion in financial characteristics drives the heterogeneous investment behavior analyzed in @sec-valuation.

![Stylized firm comparison. (a) Capital expenditure to revenue ratio (2025). The xAI-like compute racer is a pronounced outlier at 20$\times$; the other three archetypes span $0.7\times$ to $1.5\times$, with the Google-like hyperscaler above parity and the two labs at or below it. Note the broken vertical axis. (b) Revenue multiple (2025 revenue divided by 2024 revenue) versus leverage ratio. The four firm archetypes occupy distinct positions in this space, reflecting different investment strategies and financial structures.](figures/fig_firm_comparison.pdf){#fig-firm-comparison}

Several patterns emerge from @tbl-firms.
First, the xAI-like compute racer has an extraordinary investment intensity (20$\times$ revenue), reflecting a strategy of building massive training clusters before monetization; the Google-like hyperscaler also invests ahead of current demand (1.5$\times$), while the Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like labs are closer to parity.
Second, leverage is uniformly low: the two private labs are effectively all-equity funded ($\ell = 0.05$), while even the hyperscaler maintains modest leverage ($\ell = 0.10$). This low-leverage structure reflects the venture-backed nature of AI labs and the availability of equity capital at high valuations; as these firms mature and take on traditional debt (revolving credit facilities, secured notes, data center ABS), leverage ratios will rise toward the Leland framework's domain.^[The leverage ratios in @tbl-firms are round assumptions informed by qualitative evidence---Anthropic is effectively all-equity; OpenAI secured a \$4B revolving credit facility; Alphabet carries modest net debt; xAI arranged \$5B+ in secured notes and term loans (\url{https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-09/musk-s-xai-reports-higher-quarterly-loss-plans-to-power-optimus})---rather than measured market-value debt-to-capital ratios, which none of the private archetypes publishes. They should be read with the same order-of-magnitude caveat as the other firm-level inputs.]
Third, training fractions vary by approximately a factor of two across firm types (0.35 to 0.75), reflecting fundamentally different business models and beliefs about where the returns to AI compute investment will be highest.

### Baseline Results

Under the baseline calibration, the single-firm model with training-inference allocation produces an investment trigger $X^* \approx 0.0047$, capacity $K^* \approx 0.0067$, and training fraction $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, where the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-a-eff) combines L-regime inference value and H-regime training value.
By the solution convention discussed after Proposition 1, the duopoly leader's unconstrained (monopoly) policy coincides with this single-firm optimum, so $X_L^{\text{mono}} = X^* \approx 0.0047$.
The duopoly equilibrium with zero leverage produces a follower policy of $X_F \approx 0.12$, $K_F \approx 0.26$, and $\phi_F \approx 0.70$, with the leader preempting at $X_P \approx 0.0027$.
The large difference in scale between the leader ($K^* \approx 0.0067$) and the follower ($K_F \approx 0.26$, a factor of $38$) arises because the follower's contest share rises with its own capacity, so its effective elasticity of revenue to capacity is $\alpha(2 - s_F) \approx 0.48$ rather than $\alpha = 0.40$, and the capacity closed form is highly elastic at the baseline; the follower correspondingly delays entry to a demand level roughly $44$ times the preemption trigger, where the larger commitment is justified.
@sec-duopoly discusses what this asymmetry does and does not say about AI rivalry, and Internet Appendix B verifies the wedge decomposition.

The model is normalized by $c = 1$ (investment cost scale), so absolute levels of $K$ and $X$ are not directly interpretable as physical units.
The quantitative content resides in *ratios* and *percentages*: the preemption discount $X_P / X_L^{\text{mono}} \approx 0.57$ (conditional on the leader-scale convention; Internet Appendix B), the training fraction $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, the value-loss asymmetry (26\% vs.\ 6\%), and the leverage gradient of credit spreads and default probabilities (@sec-valuation).
The demand shifter $X$ and capacity $K$ are abstract state variables; only their ratios carry economic content.
To map to observable units, one would set $c$ so that $I(K) = cK^\gamma$ matches observed CapEx for a given archetype---for example, setting $c \approx \$23\text{B}$ maps the duopoly follower's investment cost $I(K_F) = K_F^{1.5} \approx 0.13$ to approximately \$3B, matching the Anthropic-like archetype's annual CapEx.
This rescaling affects no ratio, percentage, or spread reported in the paper; the model is intentionally unit-free in this sense.
All cross-environment comparisons use within-environment ratios or percentage changes, which are invariant to the cost normalization.

Strategic interaction accelerates investment: the preemption trigger $X_P \approx 0.0027$ is 43\% below the monopolist benchmark $X_L^{\text{mono}} \approx 0.0047$.
Both firms optimally allocate approximately 70\% to training ($\phi^* \approx 0.70$), reflecting the high value of the H-regime continuation payoff at the baseline arrival rate $\lambda = 0.10$; consistent with Proposition 3(ii), the training fraction is pinned down by beliefs and technology rather than by competitive position.

### Sensitivity Analysis

The following comparative statics are robust across the calibration range; @tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix reports elasticities at the baseline.
The investment trigger, capacity, and training fraction are sensitive to several key parameters.
Higher volatility $\sigma$ increases the option value of waiting, raising the investment trigger---the standard real options result that uncertainty raises the value of flexibility; for frontier AI labs, this means that higher uncertainty about future demand justifies more cautious investment timing, even as firms rush to build.
A higher discount rate $r$ reduces the present value of future cash flows through $A_{\text{eff}}$, but also raises the characteristic root $\beta_H$, lowering the option premium ratio $\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1)$; at baseline, the latter effect dominates, so the net effect is to lower both the trigger and optimal capacity; the wide variation in WACC across AI firms (10\%--18\% in our calibration) implies substantially different investment policies even for firms with identical beliefs about $\lambda$.
Higher $\lambda$ increases the weight on H-regime revenue in $A_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-a-eff), raising the effective revenue coefficient, lowering the investment trigger, and shifting the optimal training fraction $\phi^*$ upward as the expected payoff from training quality increases; the net effect is that higher $\lambda$ leads to earlier investment and a higher share of training (while single-firm $K^*$ is independent of $\lambda$ by Proposition 1, the duopoly equilibrium capacity can differ through the contest function)---consistent with the observation that more optimistic firms invest more aggressively and allocate more compute to frontier model development.
Finally, lower revenue elasticity $\alpha$ (stronger diminishing returns) reduces optimal capacity sharply, and because the smaller installation is correspondingly cheaper to build and to operate, it lowers the trigger as well: both elasticities are large and positive ($+24.2$ for capacity and $+19.7$ for the trigger; @tbl-elasticities), so at $\alpha = 0.38$ the trigger falls to $X^* \approx 0.0015$ and at $\alpha = 0.45$ it rises to $X^* \approx 0.038$, against the baseline $0.0047$.
The firm with stronger diminishing returns therefore invests earlier but at a much smaller scale.
This parameter is also crucial for the contest function specification: over the admissible range at and below the baseline, lower $\alpha$ reduces the benefit of capacity dominance in both regimes and weakens the preemption incentive, with the preemption discount $X_P/X_L^{\text{mono}}$ rising from $0.57$ at $\alpha = 0.40$ to $0.60$ at $\alpha = 0.37$.
